26-017.r: Damodar, Koel and Subarnarekha → rise on the Chotanagpur Plateau (Jharkhand).

26-018.r: Edon Canal → taken out from the Damodar river; irrigates 16,000 hectares.

26-019.r: Damodar (tributary of the Hooghly; Jharkhand, West Bengal) → tributaries Barki, Jamunia, Barakar; Indrawati is a Godavari tributary.

26-020.r: Over 90% of India's coal reserves → valleys of Damodar, Son, Mahanadi and Godavari; so 'more than one of the above'.

26-021.r: Damodar → tributary of the Hooghly (not directly of the Ganga or Padma).

26-022.r: Damodar → rises at Khamarpat Hill, Chota Nagpur Plateau.

26-023.r: Rajarappa (Chinnamastika Shakti Peeth) → confluence of Damodar and Bhera (Bhairavi), near Rajarappa falls, about 28 km from Ramgarh.

26-024.r: Damodar → east-flowing river with a rift valley formed by down-warping.

26-025.r: Not capitals: Rotterdam (Netherlands; capital Amsterdam) and Zurich (Switzerland's largest city; capital Bern). Riga → Latvia, Zagreb → Croatia are capitals.

26-026.r: Damodar → most polluted river of India; between Giridih and Durgapur it is virtually a 'biological desert' (mines, industries, cities, farms).

26-027.r: Luni → fresh upper course, saline lower course; rises in Aravalli SW of Ajmer, lost in Rann of Kutch marshes after 511 km; land-bound, never reaches sea.

26-030.r: Inland drainage (river ends in an inland lake, not the ocean) → Ghaggar, Luni, Rupen.

26-031.r: Kosi → 'Sorrow of Bihar' for its recurring floods; a transboundary river of Nepal and India.

26-032.r: Kosi → changed course in 2008 causing calamity in Bihar; 720 km in India; joins Ganga near Katihar; known for maximum course-shifting.

26-033.r: Kosi → maximum shifting of course among Indian rivers; dangerous floods; seven tributaries, Arun the most important.

26-035.r: Two Khari rivers in Rajasthan: one (Sirohi) joins Western Banas → Arabian Sea; the other (near Pushkar, Ajmer) joins Banas, a sub-tributary of the Chambal.
26-035.c: The book gives no single answer (*): the two Khari rivers belong to different drainage systems.

26-036.r: Kosi → not glacier-fed: drains Himalayan slopes in Tibet and Nepal; 720 km; joins Ganga near Katihar (Bihar); 'Sorrow of Bihar'.

26-037.r: Triveni Canal → gets water from the Gandak; located in West Champaran district.

26-038.r: Triveni Canal → built on the Gandak river in Bihar.

26-039.r: North to south → Shyok ('River of Death', Karakoram), Zaskar (joins Indus at Nimu), Spiti (from Kunzum Pass, joins Sutlej near Namgia), Satluj.

26-040.r: Hizla fair (Dumka, Santhal Pargana) → held on the bank of the Mayurakshi river.

26-041.r: India's first river-linking MoU → Ken–Betwa link between Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, signed 25 August 2005.

26-042.r: Rajghat River Valley Project (joint UP–MP) → on the Betwa, 22 km from Lalitpur (UP); Rajghat Dam is on the Betwa.

26-044.r: Only Manas–Brahmaputra is correct; Chambal joins the Yamuna near Etawah (not Narmada); Son joins the Ganga near Patna (not Yamuna).

26-045.r: A false, R true: Kali (Kalinadi) rises near Diggi (Uttara Kannada, Karnataka) and flows west into the Arabian Sea (184 km); Deccan Plateau slopes east.

26-046.r: World's highest arch bridge → on the Chenab river (India); world's highest bridge in all categories → Duge Bridge, China.

26-047.r: Mahatma Gandhi Setu → over the Ganga in Bihar, Patna (south) to Hajipur (north); 5,575 m long; inaugurated March 1982.

26-048.r: Sutlej → rises outside India at Lake Rakastal (Tibet), enters India via Shipki La (Himachal Pradesh); Beas, Chenab, Ravi rise in India.

26-049.r: Satluj → rises at Rakshastal (west of Mansarovar, Tibet; Tibetan name Langqên Zangbo); enters India through Shipki La (Kinnaur, Himachal Pradesh).

26-051.r: Ganga → Son; Godavari → Manjra; Krishna → Bhima; Yamuna → Ken.

26-052.r: Krishna → Bhima; Brahmaputra → Tista; Godavari → Indravati; Yamuna → Chambal.

26-053.r: Rapti → Ghaghra; Tista → Brahmaputra; Hiran → Narmada; Purna → Godavari (another Purna is a Tapti tributary).

26-054.r: Correct: Luni–Rajasthan (Pushkar valley near Ajmer to Rann of Kutch, 511 km). Indravati: Odisha, Maharashtra, Telangana, Chhattisgarh; Bhima: Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana; Ghatprabha: Maharashtra, Karnataka.

26-055.r: Superimposed river (keeps its course despite changes in the rocks below) → Chambal and Son are the best Indian examples.

26-056.r: Sankosh (Puna Tsang Chhu in Bhutan) → boundary between Assam and West Bengal; joins the Brahmaputra near the Assam–Bangladesh border.

26-057.r: Mahi → rises in Madhya Pradesh, enters Rajasthan at Banswara, flows south-west through Gujarat into the Gulf of Khambhat.

26-058.r: Kishan Ganga → main tributary of the Jhelum (Kishan Ganga project); Tulbul Project is also on the Jhelum.

26-059.r: Mithi river (Mumbai) → rises from Vihar Lake, joined by Powai Lake waters; flows 18 km into the Arabian Sea near Mahim Bay.

26-060.r: Sources → Cauvery: Brahmagiri Hills; Jhelum: Verinag Spring; Krishna: Mahabaleshwar; Subarnarekha: Chotanagpur Plateau.

26-061.r: Damodar → famous for fault valley drainage; flows through Jharkhand and West Bengal; called 'Sorrow of Bengal' for its floods.

26-062.r: Pen Ganga → joins Wardha, then Pranahita, then Godavari (a sub-tributary of Godavari); Mahanadi → Seonath; Damodar → Barakar; Cauvery → Bhavani.
26-062.c: Code (b) is the intended match; the book holds back only because Pen Ganga reaches the Godavari through the Wardha and Pranahita, so it is a sub-tributary, not a direct tributary.

26-063.r: Gandikota canyon ('Grand Canyon of India') → made by the Pennar, YSR (Kadapa) district, Andhra Pradesh; Telugu 'Gandi' = gorge, 'Kota' = fort.

26-064.r: Betwa → Yamuna; Kshipra → Chambal; Wainganga → Godavari; Tawa → Narmada.

26-065.r: Origins → Yamuna: Yamunotri; Krishna: Mahabaleshwar; Godavari: Nasik; Mahanadi: Sihawa.

26-066.r: Only one true: Jhelum passes through Wular Lake (island 'Zaina Lank'). Kolleru is fed by Budameru and Tammileru, not directly by Krishna; Gandak–Kanwar statement false.

27-001.r: Largest city on the Ganga → Kanpur (UA 2,920,067, Census 2011) > Patna > Varanasi > Allahabad (Prayagraj).

27-002.r: Uttarkashi → on the Bhagirathi (from Gomukh), not the Ganga; Fatehpur, Bhagalpur and Kanpur are on the Ganga.

27-003.r: Leh → right bank of the Indus (Sindhu); now in the UT of Ladakh (since 31 October 2019).

27-004.r: Ludhiana → on the old bank of the Satluj (now 13 km north of it), not the Ravi; correct: Gorakhpur–Rapti, Jabalpur–Narmada, Surat–Tapi.

27-005.r: Only row 2 right: Hundru falls → Subarnarekha, Ranchi (Chota Nagpur). Dhuandhar (Narmada, Jabalpur) is in Mahakoshal, not Malwa; Gersoppa row also wrong.

27-006.r: Bhubaneswar → on the Kuakhai (part of the Mahanadi delta), not the Mahanadi; Cuttack is on the Mahanadi.
27-006.t: Cuttack, not Bhubaneswar, stands on the Mahanadi.

27-007.r: Hyderabad → on the Musi (a Krishna tributary), not the Krishna; Vijayawada and Srisailam are on the Krishna.

27-008.r: Hyderabad → on the Musi, a tributary of the Krishna; correct: Ahmedabad–Sabarmati, Kota–Chambal, Nasik–Godavari.

27-009.r: Cuttack → Mahanadi; Ludhiana → Satluj; Nashik → Godavari; Ujjain → Kshipra.

27-010.r: Bhubaneswar → not on the Mahanadi (lies southwest of it); correct: Ahmedabad–Sabarmati, Lucknow–Gomti, Ujjain–Kshipra.

27-012.r: Betul → Tapti (rises at Multai); Jagdalpur → Indravati (south bank); Jabalpur → Narmada; Ujjain → Kshipra.

27-013.r: Govindghat → at the confluence of Alaknanda and Lakshman Ganga, not on the Mandakini; Gaurikund, Rambara, Guptakashi lie along the Mandakini.

27-014.r: Correct: Pandharpur → Chandrabhaga (Maharashtra); Tiruchirappalli → Cauvery. Wrong: Hampi (Vijayanagar capital) is on the Tungabhadra, not Malaprabha.

27-015.r: Pahalgam (Kashmir) → on the Lidder river; altitude about 2,130 m; a starting point of the Amarnath Yatra.

28-001.r: Dudhsagar → Goa; Barkana → Karnataka; Khandadhar → Odisha; Palani → Himachal Pradesh.

28-002.r: Hundru falls → on the Subarnarekha, 45 km from Ranchi; height 98 m.

28-004.r: BudhaGhagh (Lodh) Falls → on the Burha river, not Kanchi; Latehar (Jharkhand), 468 feet; correct: Hundru–Subarnarekha, Chachai–Bihad, Dhuandhar–Narmada.

28-005.r: Dudhsagar → Mandavi (Goa); Duduma → Machhkund (Koraput, Odisha); Gokak → Ghatprabha (Belagavi); Jog → Sharavati (Karnataka).

28-006.r: Correct: Jog Falls → Sharavati (Shimoga, Karnataka); Sivasamudram → Cauvery. Wrong: Kapildhara Falls is on the Narmada (Anuppur, MP), not the Godavari.

28-007.r: Bhalkund (Rahatgarh) waterfall → on the Bina river, not the Narmada; Kapildhara, Dugdhdhara and Bheraghat are on the Narmada.

28-008.r: Jog Falls → biggest waterfall in India by width, on the Sharavati (Karnataka); biggest by volume → Sivasamudram Falls (Cauvery).

28-009.r: Highest waterfall in India → Nohkalikai Falls (Meghalaya) per Meghalaya Institute of Governance; many official sources and an earlier UPPSC key say Kunchikal.
28-009.c: Sources differ: the book names Nohkalikai (not an option) as India's highest, but UPPSC has treated Kunchikal, option (b), as the highest, so (b) is the safe exam answer.

28-010.r: World Waterfalls Database: Mawsmai (Meghalaya) 315 m, Dudhsagar (Goa) 310 m, Kynrem 305 m, Meenmutty (Kerala) 300 m, Barkana 259 m, Jog 253 m.
28-010.c: By the book's database figures Meenmutty (300 m) is the tallest of the four options; UPPSC has treated Kunchikal (d) as the highest, using an older height of 455 m.

28-011.r: Jog waterfall → Sharavati, not Krishna; correct: Sivasamudram–Cauvery, Chulia–Chambal, Dhuandhar–Narmada.

28-012.r: Lodh (Budha Ghagh) falls → on the Burha river, not Barakar; Latehar; highest in Jharkhand (468 feet, 21st in India). Hundru–Swarnarekha, Jonha–Rarhu, Dasong–Kanchi correct.

28-014.r: Amritdhara waterfall → on the Hasdeo (Hasdo) river, Manendragarh-Chirmiri-Bharatpur district, Chhattisgarh; Amritdhara Festival held on Mahashivratri.

28-015.r: Chitrakote falls → 'Niagara Falls of India'; on the Indravati near Jagdalpur, Bastar (Chhattisgarh).

28-017.r: Chitrakote waterfall → Bastar district, Chhattisgarh (west of Jagdalpur), on the Indravati; called the Niagara falls of India.

28-018.r: Dudhsagar falls → Goa (Western Ghats, river Mandvi); Dhuandhar → Narmada (MP); Nohkalikai and Landshing → Meghalaya.

28-019.r: Dhuandhar Fall → at Bhedaghat (Jabalpur) on the Narmada, height 30 m, where the river passes through marble rocks.

28-020.r: Kunchikal Waterfall → 455 m (book's answer; once the tallest plunge waterfall); the World Waterfalls Database now gives 183 m.

28-021.r: Vembanad lake → Kerala's largest lake (length 83.72 km, width 14.48 km); bordered by Alappuzha, Kottayam and Ernakulam districts.

28-022.r: Periyar Lake → artificial lake fed by a river (55 km²), not a lagoon; Ashtamudi (Kerala), Chilika (Odisha) and Pulicat are lagoons.

28-023.r: Largest saline water lake → Chilika (Odisha; lagoon, 900–1165 sq km); Sambhar (Rajasthan) → largest inland salt lake; both Ramsar sites.
28-023.t: Chilika = largest saltwater lagoon; Sambhar = largest inland salt lake.

28-024.r: Chilika Lake → lagoon at the mouth of the Mahanadi on the Odisha coast, called the Northern Circars.
28-024.t: Konkan = Maharashtra's west coast; Malabar = Kerala's west coast.

28-025.r: Chilika (Odisha) → largest lagoon lake on India's east coast; Pulicat (AP–TN, west of Sriharikota) → second largest brackish lake; Kolleru → freshwater.

28-026.r: Loktak → Manipur; Didwana and Uday Sagar → Rajasthan; Kolleru → Andhra Pradesh.

28-027.r: Loktak → natural freshwater lake in Manipur, largest in Northeast India; floating islands (phumdis) carry Keibul Lamjao National Park.

28-028.r: Pulicat Lake → shared by Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh; second largest brackish water lake after Chilika.

28-029.r: Fulhar (Phulhar) Lake → Mado Tanda, Pilibhit district, Uttar Pradesh; source of the Gomati.

28-030.r: Loktak → Manipur, not Meghalaya; correct: Vembanad–Kerala, Dal–Jammu and Kashmir, Pulicat–Tamil Nadu/Andhra Pradesh border.

28-031.r: Kolleru → Andhra Pradesh; Lonar → Maharashtra, Nakki → Rajasthan, Pulicat → Tamil Nadu–Andhra Pradesh border.

28-032.r: Chapanala Lake → Assam (other Assam lakes: Chandubi, Deepor Beel, Haflong); Kolleru → Andhra Pradesh, Hamirsar → Gujarat.

28-033.r: Roopkund (glacial lake, Uttarakhand) → 'Mystery lake' or 'Skeleton lake', for hundreds of human skeletons at its edge.

28-034.r: Anchar lake → Jammu and Kashmir; Kolleru → Andhra Pradesh; Hamirsar → Gujarat.

28-035.r: Ashtamudi → Kerala; Pulicat → Tamil Nadu; Roopkund → Uttarakhand; Surajkund → Haryana.

28-036.r: Roopkund → Uttarakhand, not Himachal Pradesh; correct: Bhim Tal–Uttarakhand, Pulicat–Tamil Nadu/Andhra Pradesh, Loktak–Manipur.

28-037.r: Ghepan Lake (snow-covered, formed by a receding glacier) → Lahaul Valley, Himachal Pradesh.

28-038.r: Kayal → lagoon lake of Kerala (e.g. Punnamada, Ashtamudi, Vembanad Kayal).

28-039.r: Kodaikanal Lake (Dindigul district, Tamil Nadu) → artificial freshwater lake.

28-040.r: Sala Lake → Arunachal Pradesh; Badkhal → Haryana; Loktak → Manipur; Kaliveli → Tamil Nadu.

28-041.r: Wular → largest freshwater lake of India by water volume; by area, Kolleru is the largest.
28-041.t: By volume Wular; by area Kolleru.

28-042.r: Freshwater → Wular (Kashmir Valley) and Loktak (Manipur); Chilika → largest brackish lake; Sambhar → largest inland salt lake (Jaipur, Rajasthan); answer (e).

28-043.r: Narayani hot spring → not in Gujarat (Gujarat has 17 major hot springs, GSI); correct: Manikaran–Himachal Pradesh, Taptapani–Odisha, Vajreshwari–Maharashtra.

28-044.r: Didwana, Kuchaman, Sargol, Khatu (and Sambhar) → saline lakes of Rajasthan.

28-045.r: Telhar (Talhar) Kund waterfall → Kaimur district, Bihar, on the Rohtas Plateau.
28-045.t: It lies on the Rohtas Plateau but in Kaimur district, not Rohtas.

28-046.r: Kanwar Lake (Begusarai, Bihar) → Asia's largest freshwater oxbow lake; a Ramsar wetland.

28-047.r: Only two right: Renuka Wetland–Himachal Pradesh, Rudrasagar–Tripura; Hokera Wetland is in Jammu and Kashmir, Sasthamkotta Lake in Kerala.

28-048.r: Yaya Tso (Ladakh, about 4820 m) → 'bird's paradise'; Ladakh's first Biodiversity Heritage Site (resolved January 2023); not fed by the Sutlej.

29-001.r: 'Monsoon' → from the Arabic word 'mausim' meaning 'season'; seasonal reversal of winds that brings rain.

29-002.r: A and R true, R explains A: India's climate is monsoonal; the lofty Himalayas act as a climatic divide, shielding it from cold northern winds.

29-003.r: Map with index above 27, 25–27, 22–25, below 22 → annual mean temperature (°C); north India warmer than the south.

29-004.r: A true, R false: India has a tropical monsoon climate, but it lies between 8°4' and 37°6' N, not wholly within tropical latitudes.

29-005.r: Monsoon arrives first in Kerala; the south-west monsoon (June–September) gives India 75% of its rainfall.

29-006.r: Summer (south-west) monsoon → blows from South-West to North-East; retreating monsoon from North-East to South-West; most rain from the south-west monsoon.

29-008.r: Summer heat and low pressure over the subcontinent draw in air from the Indian Ocean → South-West monsoon, source of most of India's rain.

29-009.r: Highest salinity among options → Red Sea (about 41‰; normal open ocean 33–37‰); hot dry regions can reach 70‰.

29-010.r: Climate diagram in the question → North-East region of India.

29-011.r: Leh → driest place (least rainfall) among Mumbai, Delhi, Leh and Bengaluru.

29-012.r: January isotherm of 18°C → divides India into tropical and subtropical zones.

29-013.r: Shaded area of the map → mean July temperature 25.0°C–27.5°C.

29-014.r: Highest daily range of temperature → desert areas of Rajasthan (hot days, cold nights).

29-015.r: Tamil Nadu's main rainy season → North-East monsoon, October to December (answer: November–December).

29-016.r: Seasonal shift of the Indian monsoon → differential heating of land and sea (thermal concept); the dynamic concept was given by Flohn.

29-017.r: Both true: monsoon duration falls from south to north India; rainfall in the northern plains falls from east to west as winds lose moisture.

29-018.r: Only 2 true: IOD ('Indian Nino') is an SST difference between western and eastern Indian Ocean (not the Pacific); it can alter El Nino's effect on the monsoon.

29-019.r: False: El Nino occurs every year → it comes irregularly every two to seven years. El Nino (warm current off Peru) weakens the monsoon; La Nina strengthens it.

29-020.r: True: jet stream blows north of the Himalayas parallel to the Tibetan highlands; Tibet splits it into north and south branches. Statement 3 is false.

29-021.r: A and R true, R explains A: Agra and Darjeeling share a latitude, but Darjeeling's January is far colder; temperature falls 1°C per 165 m (normal lapse rate).

29-022.r: Amritsar and Shimla → almost same latitude; climate differs due to altitude (Amritsar about 756 feet, Shimla about 7866.10 feet).

29-023.r: Southern Chhattisgarh → Humid South-East climate (with West Bengal, Chotanagpur, Odisha plain, NE Andhra Pradesh); sub-humid transitional → eastern UP, western Bihar.

29-024.r: Chhattisgarh Basin → little affected by the Arabian Sea branch, which splits at the Western Ghats: one arm along the Aravalli (scanty rain), one blocked by the Vindhyas.

29-025.r: Humid → Kochi (3415.8 mm, 2022) and Tejpur (1775.7 mm); drier → Ludhiana (766.9 mm) and Ahmedabad (564.0 mm).

29-026.r: Retreat of monsoon → clear sky, low pressure over the Bay of Bengal, slight rise in land temperature; all three correct.

29-027.r: Only 2 true: westerlies blow between 30° and 60° in both hemispheres (not 30°N–60°S); western disturbances from the Mediterranean bring NW India's winter rain.

29-028.r: ITCZ → low-pressure trough at the equator where NE and SE trade winds meet; it shifts north or south with the sun's apparent motion.

29-029.r: Rajasthan dust storms (May–June) → only convectional currents: hot Loo winds make low pressure, and fast-rising air lifts dust.

29-030.r: Rajasthan gets little rain → winds meet no barrier to rise and cool; the Aravalli lies along the south-west monsoon direction, so west Rajasthan is a rain shadow.

29-031.r: Hindu calendar seasons → Spring (Mar–Apr), Summer (May–Jun), Rainy (Jul–Aug), Autumn (Sep–Oct), Pre-winter (Nov–Dec), Winter (Jan–Feb).

29-032.r: False: MONEX-1973 was a joint India–USSR expedition, not USA. True: Chennai's rain more variable than Mumbai's; retreating monsoon rains Tamil Nadu coast; western disturbances from Mediterranean.

29-033.r: Koppen → Cwg for the Great Plains of India (most of the Northern Ganga Plains): monsoon type climate with dry winters.

29-034.r: Koppen → North-East India including North Bengal (and Ganga Plains) → Cwg, humid sub-tropical climate with dry winter.

29-035.r: Koppen → North Bihar's climate is Cwg.

29-036.r: Koppen Amw (tropical monsoon with a short dry winter) → found mainly in the western coastal region of India.

30-001.r: India's maximum rainfall → South-West Monsoon: April–May heating creates intense low pressure in the north-west and the ITCZ shifts north.

30-002.r: Tamil Nadu → gets most rain from the North-East monsoon (about 40–50% of its annual rainfall).

30-003.r: Highest average annual rainfall among options → Sikkim (2799.2 mm, IMD 2024) > Kerala (2795.4) > Arunachal (2192.8) > J&K (873.1); Goa highest overall (4906.6).

30-004.r: Ajmer and Shillong → same latitude but huge rainfall gap: Ajmer 850.57 mm vs Shillong (East Khasi Hills) 7120.68 mm a year (2024).

30-005.r: Station with 26°C mean, 63 cm rain, 9°C annual range → Chennai (rain 60–70 cm; annual range 8–9°C).
